title: Al-Hasib, the Reckoner
hookLine: the Reckoner, and the One who is enough
tomorrow: is awe just a polite word for fear?

lines: RETURN A GREETING, OR A BETTER ONE.
cards: Someone texts hey. You send back hey!! with two exclamation points, because one felt cold. Small math, all day long: who replied fastest, who used a period, who left you on read.
The Qur'an has a verse about exactly that. In Surah An-Nisa: when you're greeted with a greeting, answer with a better one, or at least return it. Fair enough.
Then the verse ends somewhere odd. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah taketh count of all things." Why does a verse about saying hello end with God keeping count?

teach.h: THE ONE WHO KEEPS THE ACCOUNT.
teach.b: The puzzle opens on today's Name: Al-Hasib. It holds two things that sound like they pull apart. Al-Hasib is the Reckoner, the one who keeps the account, down to a returned hello.
And al-Hasib is the one who is enough, who suffices. A few verses earlier, the same surah puts both in one short line: "Allah sufficeth as a Reckoner." So here's the answer.
Nothing small goes uncounted: not the greeting, not the kindness nobody noticed. And because nothing is lost, you don't have to keep the books yourself. Your nervous scorekeeping can rest.
The friend who never texts first, the shift you covered, the thanks that never came: all of it sits on a ledger kept by Someone who doesn't miscount. The one who counts is enough.

teach.h: HASBIYALLAH, AT THE END OF THE MATH.
teach.b: That's why the phrase hasbiyallah, Allah is enough for me, belongs at the end of your own careful math, not in place of it.
In Surah Al Imran, a group is warned that a great force has gathered against them, and their faith grows instead. Their answer: "Allah is Sufficient for us! Most Excellent is He in whom we trust!"
Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Abbas says those same words were said by Ibrahim when he was thrown into the fire. Two different moments, the same few words.

how: Muslims say hasbiyallah (Allah is enough for me) or hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil (3:173) in hard moments, and are taught to return a greeting with one as good or better (4:86).

o: the one who counts all things and is enough
the one who weighs your sins against you
the one who decides who gets rich this year

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: the Reckoner, and the one who is enough
return a greeting, or a better one
said the same words in the fire

s: saying hasbiyallah means you stop planning and just wait
the people in 3:173 said it while facing a real threat. it belongs at the end of the math, not in place of it.
a verse about returning greetings ends with God taking count
"Lo! Allah taketh count of all things" (4:86, Pickthall).
Ibn Abbas says Ibrahim spoke the words of 3:173 in the fire

games.q: a friend never says thanks when you hold the door, cover a shift, send the notes. you've started a list in your head. which thought fits Al-Hasib?
o: 'every kindness is counted already. i can stop keeping score.'
'God keeps count too, so my list proves i'm right.'
'if nobody notices it, it doesn't really count.'
games.why: the Reckoner counts even a returned hello, so nothing good is lost, and the one who counts is enough. that's what lets you put your own ledger down.

practice: Say it out loud, softly, once for each worry you're carrying right now: hasbiyallah, Allah is enough for me. If you don't pray, you can say the English, or simply name each worry and set it down beside you.
Notice how each one sounds once it has been said. Then let the breath slow for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-Hasib. The Reckoner who counts all things, even a returned hello, and the one who is enough. Name forty.

orig.note: Arabic: the Reckoner, and the one who suffices. 4:6 puts both in one line: Allah sufficeth as a Reckoner.

carryVoice: Hold onto this one: he is enough, and the counting is already being done. Forty names in.
